Microsoft Extends Voluntary Buyout Offers to Roughly 60,000 Employees

Voluntary Exit Offer Reaches Select Global Markets

Microsoft has confirmed it is offering voluntary buyout packages to approximately 60,000 employees, representing about a quarter of its global workforce. The voluntary exit offer (VEO) is being extended to qualifying workers in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

According to internal guidelines communicated by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, the program is available to employees at level 70 or below within select business units. These specific organizations were chosen based on individual business priorities, ongoing customer commitments, and workforce requirements. The company characterized the program as an opportunity for individuals who may already be contemplating career transitions outside of the organization.

While Microsoft did not explicitly state a singular catalyst for the broad buyout initiative, the move follows several years of heightened capital expenditures directed toward artificial intelligence infrastructure and extensive data-center development.

Context and Prior Workforce Reductions

This initiative marks Microsoft's second voluntary workforce reduction effort of 2026. In April, the company introduced a voluntary retirement package targeted at 8,750 long-tenured U.S. employees nearing the end of their careers, approximately 30 percent of whom ultimately accepted the terms. Later in July, the Xbox division implemented a separate layoff affecting 3,200 employees, or roughly 20 percent of its gaming workforce.

Chief People Officer Amy Coleman previously noted in July that Microsoft was evaluating whether to integrate voluntary exits more regularly into its overarching workforce management strategy, building directly upon insights gained from the April retirement program.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

For eligible employees, the VEO presents a complex career decision between accepting a structured buyout package now or retaining their current positions while navigating potential future industry volatility and cost-management measures. Industry observers note that the strategy mirrors recent voluntary exit approaches utilized by other major technology firms, such as Alphabet.
